vignette: Malik, a 47-year-old African American park ranger, was deployed as a civilian aid worker in a war-torn region six years ago. He recalled a night in a ruined village when a sudden burst of gunfire erupted, and a plume of orange-red flames swept through the rubble. The sight of that fire, the echo of shouting critics among the wounded civilians, and the sense that he was standing in a landscape that felt eerily like the forest he now patrolled all became the roots of his trauma. Those memories surfaced whenever he heard a criticism, saw any flash of flame-be it a campfire or a fire alarm-or even walked along a trail that resembled the scarred paths of that war-zone village. The intensity of those triggers immediately set his heart racing, his body tightening, and made him feel as though he were back in that moment, facing danger again. The shock of those images forced him to shut down, to retreat into a shell of isolation; he began to withdraw from friends, family, and even the routine camaraderie that once defined his job. His guilt over surviving while many others did not weighed heavily on him; he felt he had violated his own sense of solidarity and compassion, and he believed that each criticism now felt like a reminder of that betrayal. The combination of the triggers, the guilt, and the sudden sense of threat left Malik with insomnia and a constant fear that something bad would happen at any moment, especially when plans were delayed or tasks took longer than expected. The realization that his own mind was amplifying danger whenever a delay occurred made even the longest walk through the park feel like a looming threat. The nightly alarms, the criticism he received from his supervisor, and the visual cue of flames at his kitchen stove all served as reminders that danger lingered. Every time these triggers flared, Malik's body reacted with a surge of adrenaline, and he felt compelled to retreat from the situation altogether. He avoided any setting that might trigger his fear: he stopped wearing his ranger uniform, avoided the police and military vehicles that passed by the park gate, and began drinking heavily after his shifts. His substance use became a refuge, a way to numb the constant vigilance that his brain demanded. Each night he poured another drink, hoping the alcohol would quiet the rumble of fear, but it only reinforced his belief that he could not relax, even in what should have been safe surroundings. He isolated himself completely, refusing visits from his sister and turning down opportunities to join the volunteer fire crew he had once loved. These maladaptive strategies fed back into his sense of isolation and amplified his survival guilt, deepening the belief that he had betrayed his values by letting his fear dictate his actions. The cycle tightened. Malik's sleep problems worsened as the days grew longer and his nights shorter; he could not let his mind stop racing until a new trigger forced him to confront the danger he feared. The more he avoided situations, the less he could practice the very relaxation techniques he had been taught during his ranger training. His avoidance of uniformed officers, in particular, reinforced his negative appraisal that he had abandoned his duty and his sense of justice. Every time a delay occurred-a delayed ranger patrol, a postponed meeting with his supervisor-his mind seized on that as a sign that catastrophe was imminent. The thought that something bad was coming made his avoidance stronger, and in turn, his avoidance reinforced the sense that danger was constant. His isolated existence made him feel even more separated from the values that had once guided him, and his sense of guilt hardened into a belief that he had become a threat to those he loved. Today, Malik has come to the clinic because he can no longer ignore the daily erosion of his life. The park is no longer a place of solace but a reminder of the fire that still blazes in his mind. He fears that if he continues on this path, he will lose his job, his health, and his sense of self. Yet he also hopes, perhaps naïvely, that talking with someone might untangle the web of triggers, guilt, and fear that keeps him locked in a cycle of isolation and avoidance.
